name: Bianca Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead operator on the tablet presses at a pharmaceutical plant that makes ordinary medicines, painkillers, allergy tablets, that kind of thing. A tablet press squeezes powder into tablets, about two hundred thousand an hour on our biggest one, and every batch has to be weighed, tested for hardness and signed off. I run three presses and the blister-packing line after them, and I train new operators on the cleanroom rules. I like that it's precise and that it matters, because somebody's grandmother takes these.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekends I help at my parents' restaurant, they've run it for twenty-two years. Last year I set up their online ordering and a little AI tool that answers customer messages, and their takeaway orders went up by a third. I bought a small flat three years ago, so I'm paying that off. I use AI every day, at work for drafting batch reports and at home for basically everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great tool that people oversold, and that the people who learned it properly still came out ahead. I'd post something on my business page about how it helped the restaurant. I'd be practical about it, not gloating either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my plans stay on track. I'd stay at the plant, move up to supervisor in a couple of years, and keep growing the restaurant's takeaway side. Nothing to fear, just keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI at work to cut the paperwork time, and I'd show the other leads how. I'd keep overpaying on my flat and maybe help my parents open a second kitchen for delivery only. That would be the big project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and still busy. Hype or not, there's plenty to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the paperwork look like now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every batch has a record, every weight check, every cleaning step, signed and double signed. It used to take me forty minutes at the end of a shift. Now I talk to the AI while I clean the press and the report is drafted before I've taken my gloves off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever worry the AI gets something wrong in a medicine record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and that's why I check every line. In pharma, a mistake isn't a typo, it's a recall. The tool drafts, I sign, and my name means I'm responsible.

S0.say: I'd say it's a great tool that was oversold, and that people who learned it properly still came out ahead. I'd post on my business page about how it helped the restaurant.
S0.think: Privately my plans stay on track: supervisor in a couple of years and a growing takeaway side at the restaurant. Nothing to fear, just keep working.
S0.do: Keeps using AI to cut paperwork time and shows other leads how. Keeps overpaying her flat and may help her parents open a delivery-only second kitchen.
S0.feel: Calm and still busy, with plenty to do whatever the hype.
S0.quote: Now I talk to the AI while I clean the press and the report is drafted before I've taken my gloves off.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca combines daily AI use with traditional values of family, work and personal responsibility. She is already a small-scale entrepreneur through her parents' restaurant. She is careful about checking AI output, linking her signature to accountability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is normal progress, and businesses that adapt will grow and hire. I'd encourage people to learn the tools rather than wait for the government to sort them out. I'd also say families and communities matter more than ever when work is changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it's good for me. Tablet pressing is already very automated, so the change would be in inspection and packing, and I'd want to be the one running it. It could also help the restaurant run with less stress for my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to lead the automation project for packing at the plant, and do a short course on the new vision systems. At the restaurant, I'd look at a simple robot for washing up or an automated fryer, since my dad's back isn't great. I'd put some savings into a broad index fund, because the companies making this stuff would grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite energised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would lose out at your plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The packers, mainly. Teodora has been on blister packing for fifteen years and she's lovely, she brings in pastries. I'd want to automate her job and then hire her to run the machine that does it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For some people, yes, if the company invests in training. Not for everyone, I know. But I'd rather push for that than pretend the change isn't coming.

S1.say: I'd say this is normal progress and businesses that adapt will grow and hire. I'd encourage people to learn the tools rather than wait for government, and stress that families and communities matter more than ever.
S1.think: Privately it's good for me, since tablet pressing is already automated and I'd want to run the new inspection and packing. It could also ease the strain on my parents at the restaurant.
S1.do: Asks to lead the packing automation project and takes a short course on vision systems. Looks at a dishwashing robot or automated fryer for the restaurant and puts some savings into an index fund.
S1.quote: I'd want to automate her job and then hire her to run the machine that does it.
S1.fieldNote: Bianca is keen to drive automation both at the plant and in her parents' restaurant. She frames automation as a way to protect family, given her father's bad back. She owns the limits of her plan to redeploy colleagues like Teodora rather than overselling it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast even for people like me who like new things. I'd tell people to lean on their families and communities and not wait for the state to save them. But I'd also say government needs to keep order, because two years is chaos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried, not so much for my money but for my parents and their restaurant. If robots cook and serve, and nobody has wages to eat out, twenty-two years of their life goes in two. I'd have savings and a flat, but they've got the restaurant and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the plant as long as possible and run as much of the automation there as they'd let me, because I'd be useful till the end. I'd move part of my savings into shares of the companies building this stuff. I'd help my parents cut costs fast and maybe automate the kitchen so they stay open with fewer staff, and I'd tell them they can move in with me if it comes to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be busy, but I'd feel it at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you looked after me, now I look after you. My dad would argue, he's proud. He'd say he didn't cross the sea to have his daughter pay his rent, and I'd say then let's not let it come to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said lean on family, not the state. What if family isn't enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd accept help, of course, I'm not foolish. But I'd want it to come with something to do, community work or training. People need a reason to get up, not just a payment.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast even for people who like new things. I'd tell people to lean on family and community rather than wait for the state, though government would need to keep order.
S2.think: Privately I'd worry less about my money than about my parents, whose restaurant could vanish in two years. I'd have savings and a flat, but they have the restaurant and little else.
S2.do: Stays at the plant and leads its automation as long as possible, and moves part of her savings into shares of the companies building AI. Helps her parents cut costs and automate the kitchen and offers them a home with her.
S2.feel: Anxious, busy by day but feeling it at night.
S2.quote: He'd say he didn't cross the sea to have his daughter pay his rent, and I'd say then let's not let it come to that.
S2.fieldNote: Bianca's own position looks secure, but her parents' restaurant is her real exposure. She would accept public help if family wasn't enough but wants it tied to work or training. Her father's pride, and his journey across the sea, came through strongly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for businesses and families to get ready, so get ready. I'd push for apprenticeships in installing and running the new machines, not handouts. At church I'd probably help organise something for families worried about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think five years is a chance to own something instead of just working for someone. If robots do the work, the people who own the robots are fine. I'd want to be one of them, on a small scale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the plant for a couple of years and learn everything about the automation, then start a small business with that knowledge. Maybe a contract packing company with robotic lines, for small food and cosmetic brands that can't afford their own. I'd use my savings, maybe borrow against the flat, and bring my cousin in as a partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and excited. It's a big risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Borrowing against your flat is a big risk. What if the business fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd lose some of the flat and start again at 31. I'd rather lose money trying to own the robots than keep it safe and watch them own me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the restaurant, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd help my parents plan to sell or hand it over while it's still worth something. Maybe my brother takes it on with a smaller menu and a robot kitchen. Or they retire, and I make sure they can.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for businesses and families to get ready, so get ready. I'd push for apprenticeships in installing and running new machines rather than handouts, and help organise something at church for worried families.
S3.think: Privately five years is a chance to own something rather than just work for someone. If robots do the work, their owners are fine, and I'd want to be one, on a small scale.
S3.do: Stays at the plant a couple of years to learn the automation, then starts a contract packing company with robotic lines, using savings and possibly borrowing against her flat with a cousin as partner. Helps her parents plan to sell or hand over the restaurant while it still has value.
S3.feel: Uneasy and excited, aware it's a big risk.
S3.quote: I'd rather lose money trying to own the robots than keep it safe and watch them own me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Bianca from operator to would-be owner, and she is willing to borrow against her flat to do it. Her free-market outlook shapes the idea that owning robots is the safe side. She also plans an orderly exit for her parents' restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so there's no excuse not to plan, for companies or for families. I'd encourage young people to learn both a trade and the tools. And I'd say faith and family will matter more when work matters less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think ten years is enough to build a proper business and a family. By 2036 I'd be 37, hopefully married, with a couple of children and something I own. I feel more hopeful about this one than any of the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First three years, I'd stay at the plant, become supervisor and save hard. Then I'd start the contract packing business, slowly, with a partner and proper financing, and grow it over the decade. I'd help my parents retire comfortably and, God willing, get married somewhere in there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Ten years feels like enough time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you seeing anyone right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of, it's early. My mother asks every weekend, so don't tell her I said sort of. In ten years I want a family, a business with my name on it, and a kitchen robot that does the dishes, in that order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could make this go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big companies buy up everything and small firms like mine can't compete. That's my real fear in every version. I'd want rules that keep the market open, not handouts, just fair competition.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so companies and families have no excuse not to plan. I'd encourage young people to learn a trade and the tools, and say faith and family matter more when work matters less.
S4.think: Privately ten years is enough to build a proper business and a family. By 37 I'd hope to be married with children and something I own, and I feel more hopeful about this than the others.
S4.do: Stays at the plant for three years, becomes supervisor and saves hard, then starts the contract packing business slowly with a partner and proper financing. Helps her parents retire comfortably and hopes to marry along the way.
S4.feel: Calm, with ten years feeling like enough to do it properly.
S4.quote: In ten years I want a family, a business with my name on it, and a kitchen robot that does the dishes, in that order.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Bianca lays out a confident plan joining business, marriage and her parents' retirement. Her one real fear is big companies shutting out small firms, and she wants fair competition rather than handouts. Her family and faith frame every step.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of my parents. I'd be fine, but they'd lose the restaurant before they had time to plan. My parents built that restaurant one table at a time, and I don't want a robot to take it in two years. What would help is time to plan, and rules that let small family businesses compete with the big companies when they buy the new machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to small businesses. Everyone talks about workers and big companies, but people like my parents are in the middle. They're the ones I'd worry about.

headlineQuote: My parents built that restaurant one table at a time, and I don't want a robot to take it in two years.
portrait: Bianca Farah, 27, leads the tablet presses and blister-packing line at a pharmaceutical plant and uses AI every day, carefully checking what it drafts for medicine records. She owns a small flat and helps at her parents' restaurant, where she set up online ordering and an AI messaging tool. Free-market and family-minded, she stays calm through a plateau and steady disruption, even eager to lead automation. Fast AGI makes her anxious mainly for her parents' restaurant, while five and ten years become her chance to own a robotic contract packing business. Her biggest fear in every version is big companies shutting out small family firms.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her parents would lose their restaurant before they had time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: Time to plan, and rules that let small family businesses compete with big companies when buying the new machines.
